questions.stem: An electron is placed between two parallel plates, with the top plate positive and the bottom plate negative. Which way is the electric force on it?
options: Upward, towards the positive plate, along the field
Parallel to the plates, perpendicular to the field
Upward, towards the positive plate, opposite to the field
Downward, towards the negative plate, along the field
questions.explanation: The field points from the positive plate to the negative plate, so it points downward. A negative charge feels a force opposite to the field, so the electron is pushed up towards the positive plate. A positive charge would be pushed down along the field.

questions.stem: Two parallel plates 2.0 cm apart have a potential difference of 500 V across them. What is the electric field strength between them?
options: 250 V m⁻¹
10 V m⁻¹
questions.explanation: E = V/d = 500/0.020 = 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Leaving the separation in centimetres gives 250 V m⁻¹, and multiplying V by d gives 10 or 1.0 × 10³, depending on the unit used for d.

questions.stem: What is the size of the force on an electron in a uniform electric field of 2.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹?
questions.explanation: F = qE = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.5 × 10⁴ ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 6.4 × 10⁻²⁴ N, and 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the charge itself, in coulombs.

questions.stem: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
questions.explanation: The work done by the field is W = qV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, and this equals the gain in kinetic energy. That is 1000 electronvolts. Treating the voltage as the energy gives 1000 J.

questions.stem: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through 1000 V. What is its final speed?
options: 3.5 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: qV = ½mv², so v = √(2qV/m) = √(2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁶/9.109 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 1.9 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the factor of 2 gives 1.3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹, and forgetting the square root gives 3.5 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻¹, faster than light. Using the proton's mass gives 4.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A proton moves from the positive plate to the negative plate of a pair of charged parallel plates. Which energy change occurs?
options: Its electrical potential energy and kinetic energy both stay the same
Its electrical potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases
Its electrical potential energy increases and its kinetic energy increases
Its electrical potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases
questions.explanation: The field does positive work on the proton as it moves along the field, so W = −ΔU and the potential energy falls while the kinetic energy rises by the same amount. An electron moving the same way would lose kinetic energy, because the force on it opposes that motion.

questions.stem: An electron enters the gap between two charged parallel plates moving parallel to them. What shape is its path while it is between the plates?
options: A straight line, because its velocity is parallel to the plates and to the field
A spiral, because its speed increases while the electric force direction keeps changing
A parabola, because it has constant velocity along the plates and constant acceleration across them
A circle, because the electric force on it is always perpendicular to its velocity
questions.explanation: The uniform field gives a constant force across the gap, so the electron accelerates uniformly in that direction while its velocity along the plates stays constant. This is the same pattern as a horizontally launched projectile, so the path is a parabola. The force does not stay perpendicular to the velocity, so the path is not a circle.

questions.stem: An electron enters a uniform field of 1.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ between plates 5.0 cm long, moving parallel to the plates at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. How far is it deflected across the gap by the time it leaves?
options: 5.5 mm
11 mm
2.2 mm
questions.explanation: The time between the plates is 0.050/2.0 × 10⁷ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ s, and the acceleration is eE/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². The deflection is ½at² = 0.5 × 1.76 × 10¹⁵ × (2.5 × 10⁻⁹)² ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻³ m. Leaving out the ½ gives 11 mm.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the strength of the magnetic field produced near a moving charged particle?
options: Bringing the particle to a stop
Halving the charge on the particle
Increasing the speed of the particle
Moving the measuring point farther away
questions.explanation: A moving charge produces a magnetic field whose strength increases with the size of the charge and its speed, and decreases with distance from the charge. A stationary charge produces an electric field but no magnetic field.

questions.stem: A charged particle moves parallel to the field lines of a uniform magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
options: The maximum force qvB, because it moves along the field lines
A force along the field lines that speeds the particle up
A force half the maximum, because it is partly aligned with the field
Zero, because sin θ = 0 when the velocity is parallel to the field
questions.explanation: F = qvB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the field. For motion along the field θ = 0, so there is no magnetic force and the particle carries on at constant velocity. The force is greatest when the velocity is perpendicular to the field.

questions.stem: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. What is the magnetic force on it?
questions.explanation: F = qvB = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ × 0.50 ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. The answer 1.0 × 10⁶ N multiplies only the speed and field and leaves out the charge, and dividing by B instead of multiplying gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹³ N.

questions.stem: A charged particle crosses a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at 30° to the field. Compared with crossing at 90° at the same speed, the force on it is:
options: the same size
√3/2 as large
twice as large
half as large
questions.explanation: F = qvB sin θ, and sin 30° = 0.5 while sin 90° = 1, so the force is halved. Using cos 30° gives √3/2, which mixes up the angle with its complement.

questions.stem: A proton moves east through a uniform magnetic field that points vertically downward. Which way is the magnetic force on it?
options: West
North
South
Up
questions.explanation: Using the right-hand palm rule, fingers along the field (down) and thumb along the proton's velocity (east), the palm pushes north. The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field, so it cannot be up or west. An electron moving east would be pushed south.

questions.stem: Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force, qvB = mv²/r, gives the radius of a charged particle's circular path. Which statement follows?
options: r = qB/(mv), so a faster particle moves in a smaller circle
r = mv/(qB), so a stronger field gives a larger circle
r = qvB/m, so a heavier particle moves in a smaller circle
r = mv/(qB), so a faster particle moves in a larger circle
questions.explanation: Cancelling one v and rearranging gives r = mv/(qB). The radius increases with mass and speed and decreases with charge and field strength, so a stronger field bends the particle into a tighter circle.

questions.stem: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.50 T magnetic field. What is the radius of its circular path?
options: 4.2 cm
8.4 cm
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB) = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2.0 × 10⁶/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.50) ≈ 0.042 m, or 4.2 cm. The value 8.4 cm is the diameter of the circle, not its radius, and slips with powers of ten give 42 m or 0.42 mm.

questions.stem: An alpha particle and a proton enter the same uniform magnetic field at the same speed, perpendicular to the field. An alpha particle has about 4 times the proton's mass and twice its charge. How do their path radii compare?
options: The alpha particle's radius is about 4 times the proton's
Their radii are equal, because their speeds are equal
The alpha particle's radius is about twice the proton's
The alpha particle's radius is about half the proton's
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB), so at the same v and B the radius is proportional to m/q. For the alpha particle m/q is 4/2 = 2 times the proton's, so its radius is about twice as large. Using mass alone gives 4 times.

questions.stem: Why does a charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field keep a constant speed?
options: The magnetic force acts along the velocity, but it is balanced by gravity
The magnetic field adds energy as fast as the particle radiates it away
The magnetic force is too weak to change the motion of a charged particle
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it does no work
questions.explanation: The force qvB is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so it changes only the direction of motion and does no work. With no change in kinetic energy, the speed is constant and the path is a circle. An electric field, by contrast, can do work on a charge.

questions.stem: Which pairing of situation and path is correct, if only the stated field acts?
options: A charge fired across a uniform magnetic field and a ball thrown horizontally both follow parabolas
A charge fired across a uniform electric field and a satellite in orbit both follow circles
A satellite in orbit and a ball thrown horizontally both have a force perpendicular to their velocity
A charge fired across a uniform electric field and a ball thrown horizontally both follow parabolas
questions.explanation: A uniform electric field and a uniform gravitational field each give a constant force in one direction, so a body launched across them follows a parabola. A charge in a magnetic field and a satellite both have a force that stays perpendicular to the velocity, giving circular motion at constant speed. The force on the thrown ball is always downward, not perpendicular to its velocity.

questions.stem: In an electron gun, what is the role of the heated cathode and the anode?
options: Electrons are released from the hot anode and accelerated towards the negative cathode
The cathode bends the electron beam, and the anode slows it down before the screen
Protons are released from the hot cathode and repelled from the positive anode
Electrons are released from the hot cathode and accelerated towards the positive anode
questions.explanation: Heating the cathode gives electrons enough energy to escape its surface (thermionic emission). The potential difference between the cathode and the positive anode accelerates them, and a hole in the anode lets a narrow, fast beam through. Each electron gains kinetic energy qV.

questions.stem: In a velocity selector, crossed electric and magnetic fields let through only ions moving at one speed. With E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.15 T, what speed passes undeflected?
questions.explanation: The ion passes straight through when the electric and magnetic forces balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 3.0 × 10⁴/0.15 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Multiplying E and B gives 4.5 × 10³, and dividing B by E gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁶.

questions.stem: In a mass spectrometer, ions of the same charge and speed enter a uniform magnetic field. How does the field separate two isotopes?
options: The heavier isotope moves in a circle of smaller radius
The heavier isotope is slowed down more by the field
The lighter isotope passes straight through undeflected
The heavier isotope moves in a circle of larger radius
questions.explanation: With q, v and B the same, r = mv/(qB) is proportional to mass, so heavier ions curve less tightly and land farther along the detector. The magnetic force does no work, so it does not slow either isotope.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the functions of the fields in a mass spectrometer?
options: An electric field bends the ions in a circle, and a magnetic field slows them down
A magnetic field gives the ions their charge, and an electric field sorts them by size
An electric field accelerates the ions, and a magnetic field bends them by different amounts
A magnetic field accelerates the ions, and an electric field bends them in a circle
questions.explanation: The ions are accelerated by an electric field (gaining energy qV), often pass through a velocity selector, and are then bent into circular paths by a uniform magnetic field, with r = mv/(qB) depending on mass. A magnetic field cannot speed ions up, because its force is perpendicular to their motion.

questions.stem: Why does a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experience a force?
options: The current heats the conductor, which then expands across the field lines
The external field produces an electric field that repels the conductor
The magnetic field of the current interacts with the external magnetic field
The external field adds extra electrons, which pull the conductor along
questions.explanation: A current produces its own magnetic field around the conductor. Where this adds to the external field the combined field is stronger, and where it opposes the external field it is weaker, and the conductor is pushed from the stronger region towards the weaker. Equivalently, each moving charge in the wire feels a force qvB.

questions.stem: The force on a straight current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field is F = lIB sin θ. What is θ?
options: The angle between the conductor and the force on it
The angle between the force and the magnetic field
The angle the conductor turns through each second
The angle between the conductor and the magnetic field
questions.explanation: θ is the angle between the direction of the current in the conductor and the field. The force is greatest when they are perpendicular and zero when the conductor lies along the field. The force itself is always perpendicular to both the conductor and the field.

questions.stem: A 0.25 m length of wire carries 4.0 A at right angles to a 0.30 T magnetic field. What force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = lIB = 0.25 × 4.0 × 0.30 = 0.30 N. The answer 3.3 N divides by the field instead of multiplying, and 0.075 N leaves out the current.

questions.stem: A wire carrying 4.0 A lies at 30° to a 0.30 T field, with 0.25 m of its length in the field. What force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = lIB sin θ = 0.25 × 4.0 × 0.30 × sin 30° = 0.15 N. Using cos 30° gives 0.26 N, and 0.30 N is the force when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current towards the east through a horizontal magnetic field pointing north. Which way is the force on the wire?
options: Towards the south
Vertically upward
Vertically downward
Towards the west
questions.explanation: With the right-hand palm rule, fingers north along the field and thumb east along the current, the palm faces up, so the force is vertically upward. The force must be perpendicular to both the current and the field, which rules out every horizontal direction.

questions.stem: Which change would NOT increase the force on a straight wire lying at right angles to a uniform magnetic field?
options: Turning the wire so it lies at 45° to the field
Increasing the current in the wire
Using a stronger magnetic field
Putting a longer section of wire in the field
questions.explanation: F = lIB sin θ. Increasing l, I or B increases the force. At 90° sin θ is already at its maximum value of 1, so turning the wire to 45° reduces the force to about 71% of its value.

questions.stem: A spanner is 0.25 m long. A force of 40 N is applied at its end at right angles to the handle. What is the torque?
options: 40 N m
10 N m
160 N m
questions.explanation: τ = rF sin θ = 0.25 × 40 × sin 90° = 10 N m. Dividing the force by the length gives 160, and 40 N m forgets to multiply by the distance from the pivot.

questions.stem: The same 40 N force is applied to the end of a 0.25 m spanner, but at 30° to the handle. What is the torque?
options: 10 N m
2.5 N m
5.0 N m
8.7 N m
questions.explanation: τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the radius (the handle) and the force: 0.25 × 40 × sin 30° = 5.0 N m. Using cos 30° gives 8.7 N m. Only the perpendicular component of the force produces torque.

questions.stem: A rectangular coil of 50 turns, area 0.020 m², carries 2.0 A in a 0.40 T field. What is the torque when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field?
options: 40 N m
0 N m
questions.explanation: When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, its normal is perpendicular to the field, so sin θ = 1 and the torque is greatest: τ = nIAB = 50 × 2.0 × 0.020 × 0.40 = 0.80 N m. The torque is zero when the plane is perpendicular to the field. Leaving out the number of turns gives 0.016 N m.

questions.stem: The same coil (50 turns, 0.020 m², 2.0 A, 0.40 T) is turned so that the normal to its plane is at 30° to the field. What is the torque now?
questions.explanation: τ = nIAB sin θ, with θ the angle between the field and the normal to the coil: 0.80 × sin 30° = 0.40 N m. Using cos 30° gives 0.69 N m, which would be correct only if 30° were measured between the field and the plane of the coil.

questions.stem: What does the split-ring commutator do in a simple DC motor?
options: Reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the torque keeps the same direction
Keeps the current in the coil flowing in the same direction so the coil can rotate
Converts the direct current supply into alternating current for the field magnets
Holds the coil in place so that it cannot touch the field magnets as it spins
questions.explanation: Without a commutator, the torque on the coil would reverse after each half turn and the coil would rock back and forth. The split ring swaps the coil's connections to the supply each half turn, reversing the current in the coil so the torque always turns it the same way.

questions.stem: How does a simple AC motor with slip rings differ from a simple DC motor with a split-ring commutator?
options: The slip rings replace the brushes, so the AC motor needs no sliding electrical contacts
The slip rings convert the AC supply into direct current before it reaches the rotor coil
The slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same supply terminal, and the AC supply reverses the current
The slip rings reverse the current every half turn, and the AC supply keeps the current flowing one way
questions.explanation: Slip rings are two separate rings, so each end of the coil always connects to the same terminal. The current in the coil reverses because the supply itself alternates, and in a simple AC motor the coil turns in step with the supply. Brushes still press on the slip rings to make contact.

questions.stem: In a simple brushed DC motor, what is the function of the brushes?
options: To keep sliding electrical contact between the supply and the rotating commutator
To slow the coil down so that it turns at a steady speed
To produce the magnetic field that the rotor coil turns in
To clean dust off the coil so that it stays a good conductor
questions.explanation: The coil rotates but the supply wires are fixed, so carbon brushes press against the commutator to keep the circuit complete as it turns. The field comes from the field magnets or field coils, not the brushes.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the maximum torque of a simple brushed DC motor?
options: Reducing the current through the rotor coil
Using weaker field magnets on either side
Making the rotor coil's area smaller
Winding more turns of wire on the rotor coil
questions.explanation: τ = nIAB sin θ, so the torque increases with the number of turns, the current, the coil's area and the field strength. Curved pole pieces and an iron core also help, by making the field radial so the coil's plane stays parallel to the field for more of each turn.

questions.stem: An electron and a proton, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. Which statement is correct?
options: The proton gains more kinetic energy, because it is about 1800 times heavier
The electron gains more kinetic energy, because it is accelerated more quickly
They gain the same kinetic energy, but the electron ends up much faster
They gain the same speed, but the proton ends up with more kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Both have charge of size e, so the field does the same work qV on each and they gain equal kinetic energy. Since ½mv² is the same and the electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, the electron's speed is about 43 times greater. Mass affects the speed reached, not the energy gained.

questions.stem: A proton moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, what happens to the time it takes to complete one circle?
options: It quarters, because the magnetic force on the proton doubles
It stays the same, because the radius doubles along with the speed
It halves, because the proton is moving twice as fast around the circle
It doubles, because the radius of the circle doubles as well
questions.explanation: The period is T = 2πr/v, and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB), which does not depend on speed. Doubling the speed doubles the radius, so the proton travels twice as far at twice the speed and takes the same time.
